rv.q: Now “Plenty” is back at the Public and, if anything, the drama about a woman’s journey from wartime adventure to postwar disenchantment seems even more prescient about world politics and trenchant about the dismantling of the psyche of this challenging woman.
It’s a signal event, a comprehensively satisfying production that features a blowtorch-hot performance by Rachel Weisz.
Although the play’s original impact has been blunted with time, this slick revival directed by David Leveaux respects the historical moment.
Because the play works on so many levels and delights in so many ambiguities, it requires a firm sense of place and time and purpose, which David Leveaux’s revival does not offer.
The plenitude of Hare's play is not well served by this production's postures of austerity.
It is what makes the play, even in a production that's only good, great.
Neither Weisz nor her director David Leveaux meets that challenge in this revival, which in both her character and in the sense of overall emotional impact is somewhat chilly.
Like many mavericks who once shocked the world, she has aged into a bit of a bore.
Neither director David Leveaux nor Rachel Weisz in the lead role satisfyingly meets the challenges of this structurally complex drama in the Public Theater's torpid revival.
Hare's play thrills and unnerves yet for showing us how all-consuming darkness can develop from humanity's brightest accomplishments.
"Plenty" is an old-fashioned play of the best kind: solidly built, intelligent, thoughtful and provocative.
Rachel Weisz is electrifying as Susan Traherne...Weisz can't save the play's more plodding moments.

Rachel Weisz is mesmerizing in the first New York revival of “Plenty,” the 1978. David Hare drama about a female British secret agent whose dissatisfying post-war life drives her slowly mad -- but the award-winning actress would have been better served by a more coherently directed and designed production.
Plenty is still very much worth seeing, even in a production that doesn't realize its full potential.
The play suffers, however, from Hare’s eagerness to turn Weisz’s character into an ideological mouthpiece and her childlessness into a heavy-handed metaphor.
Leveaux's stilted and slow-moving production supplies little for her to bounce off.
That said, the play is slow, depressing and jumbled, leaving little reason to bring it back other than to serve as a star vehicle.
Certainly, Hare’s drama doesn’t play as well as memory serves.
Plenty becomes a distinctly hard play to follow when there's not much to latch onto.
This production, directed by David Leveaux, certainly doesn't make it clear.

Of all the crazed, destructive, female characters that the stage has given us, Susan Traherne may be among the least interesting, at least as performed by Rachel Weisz in the Public Theater revival of Plenty.

Far more than a vibrant assertion of the enduring value of Hare's work — an exploration of the decline of British optimism and moralism in the decades after World War II — this "Plenty" is mostly just a handsomely designed bore.
Like its lead character, the production fails to recapture the excitement of the moment of its creation.
Watching the tedious production that opened at The Public Theater this week, however, I had to wonder: could it, after all?
Plenty is crazy beauty in these ashes.
Susan’s slow mental deterioration, brilliantly portrayed by the exceptional Rachel Weisz, mirrors the British post-war disillusionment and depression, and is as exciting as it is devastating.
Rachel Weisz gives a deeply affecting performance in a role that matches Ibsen’s Hedda Gabler in its complexity.
Weisz gives a fabulous performance as she falls further and further into emotional trauma.
An imperfect if often riveting piece of theater, Plenty does leave plenty of things for us to think about.
In the case of Plenty, the revival of the David Hare drama that is running at The Public Theater through Dec. 1, the miscasting of the two ledes has thrown the entire production off-balance.
The explosions have diminished into sparklers, and the grip has, well, lost its grip.
The problem is Weisz, who is normally so warm and empathetic is so chilly you can feel the frost.
Why Plenty was chosen is a mystery.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this Hare revival, with Rachel Weisz earning praise for an electrifying performance in a challenging role, but many find the production itself flawed and the once-revolutionary play has lost much of its original impact.
